title: Pocahontas and the voice of the wind.
lines: Long ago, in a big green land, a people lived by a river.
They lived close to nature.
They hunted, fished and planted corn.
The chief's daughter was called Pocahontas.
She had long black hair that blew in the wind.
Pocahontas was free and curious.
She ran through the forest.
She jumped from high rocks into the river.
She paddled her canoe.
She had two animal friends.
Meeko the raccoon.
He ate everything he found.
And Flit, a little hummingbird with a long beak.
Pocahontas often went to a very old tree.
Grandmother Willow.
The tree had a face and could talk.
She gave wise advice.
Listen to the wind, said Grandmother Willow.
The wind will show you the way.
One day Pocahontas saw something strange on the sea.
A big ship with white sails.
Men got off it, with helmets and heavy clothes.
They had come from very far away across the sea.
They were looking for gold.
One of those men was John.
He had blond hair and blue eyes.
He saw Pocahontas by the waterfall.
They didn't speak the same language.
But Grandmother Willow said: Listen with your heart.
And then they understood each other.
Pocahontas showed John the forest.
Look, she said.
Everything is alive.
The trees.
The river.
The clouds.
All the animals are our brothers and sisters.
John had never looked at nature like that.
He learned a lot from it.
But the other men wanted to chop down trees and dig up the land.
And Pocahontas's people wanted the strangers to leave.
Both groups got angry.
They wanted to fight.
Pocahontas ran to Grandmother Willow.
What should I do?
Listen to the wind, said the tree.
The wind blew.
Leaves swirled around Pocahontas.
She ran to the hill where everyone was ready to fight.
She stood between the two groups.
Stop!
she shouted.
If you fight, everyone loses.
Look at each other.
We can be friends too.
It went quiet.
Her father put down his weapon.
Then everyone did.
The men and Pocahontas's people ate corn together.
Meeko ate all the sailors' biscuits.
And the wind blew softly through the leaves of the trees.
The end.
